title: Reasoning by analogy
hookLine: extending a ruling to a new case by a shared reason

cards: A woman from the tribe of Juhayna comes to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Her mother had vowed to make the pilgrimage, and died before she could go. May the daughter go for her?
In Sahih al-Bukhari, the answer is yes, and the way he answers is the point. He asks her back: if your mother had owed a debt, would you have paid it? Yes, she says.
Then pay what is owed to Allah, for Allah has more right to be paid. A case she understood, a debt, carried over to one she didn't, by what the two shared. Today's word is that move.

teach.b: The word is qiyas, measuring one thing against another.

In Sunni legal theory it names a way of reaching a ruling for a new case no text addresses directly, by finding an old case a text does address, and a reason the two share. Its parts: the root, the asl, the original case.
The branch, the far', the new case. The 'illa, the shared reason behind the ruling.
And the hukm, the ruling itself, which travels from root to branch along that reason.

teach.h: WINE, AND THE REASON BEHIND IT.
teach.b: An example the books reach for is wine. The Qur'an names strong drink among the things believers are told to leave aside, in Surah al-Ma'idah, verse ninety. Jurists asked what it is about wine that carries the ruling.
Not the grape. Not the color. The intoxication.
So when a drink made from something else intoxicates the same way, the ruling reaches it too, by likeness.
A hadith in Sahih Muslim says directly that every intoxicant is forbidden, and jurists treat that report as its own text; the wine case is still how the books teach the method.

Qiyas isn't a hunch or new law out of nowhere. It starts from a text and travels only as far as the reason travels. If the shared reason is wrong, the analogy fails, and much of the scholars' arguing is over exactly that.
Not every school uses it the same way.

teach.h: THE SCHOOLS DON'T ALL USE IT.
teach.b: The Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali schools count it as a source. Ja'fari jurists, of the Shia, don't reason by analogy in this way; they give reason its own place, and that's tomorrow.

how: In the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali schools, jurists use analogy to rule on cases no text names, by finding a shared reason with a case a text does name; Ja'fari jurists do not reason by analogy in this way.

games.q: a daughter asks the Prophet whether she may make the pilgrimage her late mother vowed. how does he answer?
o: he tells her a vow ends with the one who made it.
he asks whether she would pay her mother's debt.
he tells her to ask the scholars of her tribe.
games.why: he asks about a debt. she would pay it, so, he says, pay what is owed to Allah. the answer is yes, reached by likeness.

practice: Take a rule you already keep, like not reading someone's private messages, and name its reason: they're theirs, and weren't opened to you.
Then find a new case that shares the reason, a diary left on a table, and see whether the reason travels; if it does, the rule travels with it. If you pray, you can ask for clear sight.

wordCard.voice: Qiyas. Reasoning by analogy: a ruling carried from an old case to a new one, along the reason they share. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: measuring one thing against another; in law, reasoning by analogy.

carryVoice: Your line: by likeness. A ruling travels only as far as its reason. See you tomorrow.
